stories.headline: NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, MLS urge action against threats from bettors
stories.summary: The NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, MLS and their players' unions are urging state gambling regulators to combat escalating harassment and violent threats from sports bettors.
stories.body:
The five largest American professional sports leagues and their players' unions are urging state gambling regulators to combat escalating harassment and violent threats from sports bettors.

The NFL, NBA, Major League Baseball, NHL, Major League Soccer and their respective players' unions on Tuesday sent a letter to gambling regulators in 35 states and the District of Columbia, proposing a lifetime ban from legal sportsbooks for individuals who harass or threaten professional or amateur athletes, coaches, officials, team personnel or their families.

The leagues and unions want states to establish a streamlined reporting mechanism, allowing evidence of threats to be transmitted to regulators and law enforcement. Anyone found to have violated the policy would be placed on a sportsbook exclusion list shared among states.

"Too often, individuals who lose sports bets direct threatening and harassing messages toward players, coaches, and their families via social media and in-person interactions," the leagues' letter states. "Threatening the safety of an athlete or their family members over a sports bet crosses a bright ethical and criminal line, and it is entirely unacceptable."

Last May, pitcher Lance McCullers, then with the Houston Astros, said he received threats on social media to "find my kids and murder them" after a rough performance against the Cincinnati Reds. An investigation by Houston police determined an intoxicated bettor overseas was behind the threats.

Four states -- Louisiana, Ohio, West Virginia and Wyoming -- already have similar policies in place, and some of the largest sportsbooks have taken steps to combat the issue. DraftKings and Fanatics partnered with Integrity Compliance 360 this summer to implement a technology that uses artificial intelligence and investigative tools to detect social media abuse and identify the people behind it.

"It's just an infuriating issue," Matt King, CEO of Fanatics Betting and Gaming and a sports betting industry veteran, told ESPN in June.

Houston Rockets guard Fred VanVleet, president of the NBPA, said players are still adjusting to the new betting environment surrounding sports.

"We carry all of the burden, all of the risk and danger that comes with the association to gambling," VanVleet said in July. "It was one of those things that was just kind of thrown upon us, and I think everybody's trying to figure out how to adjust to it."

stories.headline: 'The Hoop Collective': Episodes of Brian Windhorst's NBA podcast
stories.summary: Here are the top highlights from Brian Windhorst's "The Hoop Collective" podcast, from breaking news to the latest intel and reaction from around the NBA.
stories.body:
"The Hoop Collective" podcast, hosted by ESPN's Brian Windhorst, releases episodes every Monday, Wednesday and Friday during the NBA season and Tuesday and Friday during the offseason. Windhorst and his guests break down what's happening on and off the court, evaluating the trends you need to know and examining the latest news from across the NBA.

Listen to 'The Hoop Collective':

ESPN | Spotify | YouTube | Apple | Amazon | iHeartMedia | TuneIn

'The Hoop Collective' episodes

Sept. 15: Ballmer punishment accepted, Kawhi trade completed and owner meetings ahead

Brian is joined by ESPN's Vincent Goodwill and Tim MacMahon to discuss LA Clippers' owner Steve Ballmer accepting the NBA's punishment and how that led to the completion of the Kawhi Leonard trade to the Toronto Raptors. The trio breaks down what to expect from Leonard on the court and if we'll see an elite performance out of him once again. They then close on the NBA owners' meetings, including the state of expansion in the NBA.

Sept. 8: What history may tell us about Clippers' future + key signings in the West
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to cover the latest fallout from the LA Clippers' punishment after the NBA announced its punishments for the franchise's off-the-court dealings with Kawhi Leonard. They discuss what league history could tell us about what's ahead for the Clippers and how LA got into this situation. They then close on key deals in the West, including Ben Simmons signing with the Sacramento Kings and Amen Thompson's extension with the Houston Rockets.

Topics:

0:27: Updates on the fallout from Clippers' punishment

6:37: Past may be an indicator of the future in LA

12:36: What did Kawhi know about these deals?

14:49: How LA got here trying to take over the city

23:28: Amen Thompson signs extension with Rockets

32:09: Ben Simmons signs with the Kings

40:19: Brian's soccer trip through London

Windhorst on the league's reaction to the Clippers' punishment: "I think Steve Balmer had support of his peers in this, even though these was pretty severe accusations.

"I'm not saying everybody again, but I think people wanted to believe him, his peers. I'm not talking about the other GMs. I'm not talking about the agents. ...

"So the word that was said to me by a very influential person was that the other owners, some of the other owners were aghast when they read this report. That was the word that was used to me, aghast. And regardless of what Steve says, the support that he had is no longer there."

Windhorst on the Clippers' best course of action now: "When the Wolves were found guilty, Glen Taylor said words that were not, "I'm guilty." Kevin McHale, who was the vice president of basketball operations, said, 'I didn't even know this existed.' You know, he pled ignorance.

"[Then] They thought about it. They ended up negotiating with the league office and they pled guilty. And two days after basically they raised the white flag in December, David Stern gave him back a pick and a year later he gave him back the second pick. Now he gave them back -- he took away five years of picks [previously] -- he gave them back Year 3 at first and then Year 5. It wasn't like he gave him back immediately. But I think the Clippers should study that."

MacMahon on why Houston extended Thompson now: "I've been telling you for a while just how much the Rockets value Thompson. If there's one untradeable player on the roster, it is him.

"According to their metrics, they think he's one of the top 10 -- and I might be inflating that number -- most valuable players in the league. Now, we can argue and we can debate and you can say that's ridiculous. I'm just telling you the way that they view him. And so for them to get a player they value that much on this deal is great value for them.

"And for Amen Thompson, $208 million fully guaranteed and there's no options either way in the deal, he's set for life. He wants to be in Houston. He's going to be in Houston."

Sept. 3: EMERGENCY POD: NBA announces Clippers' punishments after Kawhi probe
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon to react to the hefty punishments handed down to the LA Clippers by the NBA after the investigation into Kawhi Leonard's off-court dealings. They break down what this means for the future of the Clippers, if the punishment makes sense and if this will impact Leonard's pending trade to the Toronto Raptors.

Topics:

1:25: NBA punishes Clippers after Kawhi probe

7:04 :The Clippers' argument against the NBA in this

10:36: What sticks out about the NBA's findings

16:47: What comes next for the Clippers?

30:21: How will this punishment impact Kawhi?

32:56: Who was most impacted by this punishment?

43:56: Final thoughts on this punishment decision

MacMahon on why the penalty was so large for the Clippers: "The simple fact of the matter is this ain't the first time Steve Balmer's pulled this shady stuff. That did not help his case.

"They gave him a little slap on the wrist for the DeAndre Jordan stuff in 2015. $250,000 fine. It was 'Oh, whoops. We didn't know.' And then, there's the investigation for the Kawhi signing because, guess what? It's not like Uncle Dennis only asked the Clippers for a whole bunch of under-the-table stuff. He was asking everybody for under-the-table stuff. 'Oh, geez. You know, we were asked, but we didn't, you know, didn't give him anything' and and now this. So, in a way they're three-time losers."

Windhorst on the Clippers' best course of action following the ruling: "If they could get an agreement, if they could plead guilty, get an agreement and and say, 'We're not going to challenge any of these penalties.' And they get an agreement that there'll be no further penalties -- basically, they'll say that these five first-round picks are all-encompassing, they cover everything. It's a blanket agreement and [then] they keep their nose clean, and they do the Kawhi trade, they might be able to come out of this without four broken limbs. They may be able to come out of this with less damage."

MacMahon on one of the winners of the investigation: "I do think Adam Silver in a way is a winner of this because straight up, he had been soft on crime as the commissioner since, ironically, he booted the previous Clippers owner, which was completely different circumstances."

Sept. 1: How Steph Curry can decide Warriors' future and major questions for Pistons
Brian is joined by ESPN's Tim MacMahon and Anthony Slater to discuss Stephen Curry's future with the Golden State Warriors, including how a potential extension could determine the franchise's outlook. They then move on to the Jalen Duren-Detroit Pistons situation, as his restricted free agency continues. Will this cause major issues for the Pistons' season? They close on the recent dramatic FIBA World Cup qualifiers, including a matchup between Victor Wembanyama and Nikola Jokic.

Topics:

2:09: Latest on Steph Curry's future in Golden State

8:31: How Steph could help the Warriors' chances

20:16: Jalen Duren and Pistons still stuck in negotiations

26:13: What is the worst-case scenario for Detroit?

40:40: Windy Storytime: Cavs contract standoff

46:06: Headlines from FIBA World Cup qualifiers

46:48: Epic battle between Wembanyama and Jokic

49:39: Other NBA stars making an impact in FIBA

Slater on the potential Curry extension in Golden State and why he could wait: "One of the things in discussions I've been having with people is this idea of, let's say he's like, '[Taking less money for the team is] something I'd think about.' I would be surprised if he locked into a number now because, as you just saw with Draymond Green, the Warriors and their legendary figures are willing to trust each other in business.

"Draymond Green willingly gave up $27 million and went into unrestricted free agency where he couldn't have got $27 million back, [but] under the understanding if business didn't work out, he would get that money back. If you're Steph, you say, 'OK, you know what? I'll give y'all a crack at going and trying to find some stuff, but if you don't, at the end of the day, if I come back and say, give me the full max, I get the full max.'

"So, to answer your question, he doesn't have to necessarily lock into it now because they can't really execute [upgrading the roster]. Even if they could say, 'Hey, here's a theory of what we could do. Here's another theory of what we could do,' he could just say, 'All right, well, I'll hold off for now and see if you can do it, but at the end of the day, if I want the max, give me the max.'"

MacMahon on the Duren-Detroit situation: "He just averaged 19 [points] and 11 [rebounds]. He's a big physical force with some skill. Unfortunately, and this is part of the complications here, is he also just had a really disappointing playoff performance. I would say in terms of individual playoff performances coming off of that All-NBA season, Jalen Duren might have been the most disappointing in the league.

" ... I've talked to just executives from other teams around the league just kind of taking people's temperature and a lot of what I got is like, 'I can definitely see both sides of this,' because for the Pistons this is not an anti-Jalen Duren thing. This is a, 'We want to keep this core together.' By the way, they're also in the process of attempting to negotiate an extension with Ausar Thompson."

MacMahon on the Wembanyama-Jokic rivalry: "As much as Denver's summer was frankly a disaster, you can't just dismiss the Nuggets.

"Let me say this, Victor Wembanyama might be the most dominant defensive player in the history of the game. One guy he does not bother much is Nikola Jokic. Do you know what Joker's stats against Wemby are in seven games in the NBA? 37.3 points per game, 10.9 rebounds, 9.1 assists."

stories.headline: Drake Batherson signs 8-year, $86M extension with Senators
stories.summary: Senators forward Drake Batherson has signed an eight-year, $86 million extension through the 2034-35 season.
stories.body:
Ottawa Senators forward Drake Batherson has signed an eight-year, $86 million extension with the team through the 2034-35 season, it was announced Tuesday.

The deal carries an average annual value of $10.75 million per season.

"Drake exemplifies what it is to be an Ottawa Senator," general manager and president of hockey operations Steve Staios said. "He was drafted and developed by our organization and has shown a commitment to wanting to be in Ottawa long term. We view him as a key part of our core group."

Batherson, 28, is only the second player in league history to increase his individual points total in seven consecutive seasons. He had 33 goals and 38 assists in 79 games last season, and he also led the Senators with four points in four postseason games.

stories.headline: Small changes in biggest weight class in MMA divisional rankings
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
The UFC's heavyweight division appears to be stuck in neutral gear.

It's not just about Tom Aspinall vacating the championship on Monday because he is still recovering from an eye injury suffered in last October's no-contest in a title defense against Ciryl Gane. Gane, who won the interim championship with a knockout of Alex Pereira in June, remains atop the ESPN rankings. The top 10 still features Aspinall -- he's eligible to be ranked until the middle of next month, when he will have been inactive for a year -- and includes two heavyweights from outside the UFC in the top six (Francis Ngannou, Vadim Nemkov).

The heavyweight rankings underwent small changes as a result of Saturday's UFC matchup of top-10 fighters Waldo Cortes Acosta and Curtis Blaydes. Cortes Acosta entered the weekend ranked sixth, but after losing by unanimous decision, he drops to No. 9. Blaydes is one spot above him, moving up from 10th.

The only other movement in the divisional rankings is at women's flyweight, where former UFC champion Alexa Grasso moves up one position to No. 4 after Saturday's unanimous decision win over Manon Fiorot. Formerly ranked second, Fiorot drops three spots after her first loss in a nontitle bout since her pro debut in 2018.

stories.headline: How the Washington Mystics went from rebuild to playoffs in two years
stories.summary: The Mystics are riding a wave of talented young players and exuberance to the WNBA playoffs.
stories.body:
WASHINGTON D.C. -- AT any given moment with the Washington Mystics, a dance party can break out. Rookies Lauren Betts and Cotie McMahon instantly start to rock when Tyler, The Creator's "Sticky" plays at practice, mouthing the lyrics as they stand on the sideline.

The next day at shootaround, it's Betts and assistant coach Barb Turner shaking to Blac Youngsta's "Booty." Kiki Iriafen, McMahon and Georgia Amoore join in when "Super Gremlin" by Kodak Black comes on. Even coach Sydney Johnson will break out his own ... unique moves after victories.

It's all fun and games the late August day before the Mystics take on the Toronto Tempo -- until someone blows a defensive assignment in practice. That's when the bass comes out of the typically mild-mannered Johnson's voice, who laments that Marina Mabrey will hit that open jumper every time.

Things have drastically changed in the past 23 months for the youthful Mystics, playoff-bound for the first time since 2023. With six first-round picks from the past two drafts and a sprinkle of veteran leadership, the lightning-quick franchise rebuild has created a playful-yet-serious vibe that just seems to fit this particularly constructed roster. There's even the nickname that would be considered derogatory if they didn't give it to themselves (think of a garden tool that rhymes with rose).

"Young h-s, we are fun," McMahon said, barely containing her laugh. "Don't take anything serious unless we're on the court. This is an amazing group of girls. This is honestly like daycare, you know. We come here for the day, work out, have fun. Then we go back home and it's like, oh, so boring.

"The coaches had to adjust to us. They had to figure out how to deal with us and how to handle us. Some of the things we say, they can't do anything but laugh."

Shakira Austin, an elder stateswoman at 26, added, "Them girls, they crazy."

The girls might be crazy, but they've already become the youngest playoff team in WNBA history just two years into a rebuild that began before the 2025 season. Mike Thibault, at the time the winningest coach in league history, was fired as general manager and his son Eric was let go as coach. The two had been with the organization since 2013 -- Mike was coach for 10 seasons before being followed by Eric -- advancing to the 2018 Finals and winning the title in 2019.

Four years later, former Los Angeles Clippers GM Michael Winger was hired as the president of Monumental Basketball, which owns the Washington Wizards and Mystics. He was fairly hands-off in 2023 and 2024, primarily focused on the Wizards. That changed in 2025. The Thibaults were let go, and the proverbial house was cleaned. Austin and head of domestic scouting Shelley Patterson are, essentially, the only two remaining from the previous regime. Jamila Wideman was hired as the new GM and lasted all of one season.

As the reorganization took place on and off the court, one thing emerged: Winger would be the ultimate decision-maker, even when Wideman was on staff. The draft-and-develop strategy first employed by the Wizards was eventually tailored to fit the Mystics. But while the Wizards had the worst three-year stretch in franchise history, the Mystics' youngsters have had an immediate impact on winning.

Six first-round draft picks in the last two years produced youthful depth: a pair of All-Stars in Sonia Citron and Kiki Iriafen, both in their sophomore season; a rookie starting point guard in two-time all-American Georgia Amoore (she missed the 2025 season with an ACL injury). Betts, the two-time all-American and 2026 NCAA tournament Final Four Most Outstanding Player, comes off the bench. Angela Dugalic and Cotie McMahon were also first-round selections in May.

"It's not fun if everybody around you isn't having fun," Iriafen said. "Honestly, some days it feels like we're in college again. Like, we come into practice and we hang out in the locker room. Then we're like, let's go get matcha. Or on the road, we're like, oh, who wants to come to the movies with me?

"So we definitely have a chemistry off the court that has just bled into on the court."

THIS SEASON'S ROSTER almost looked very different.

Austin, the 2022 No. 3 overall pick, could have been somewhere else entirely. She signed a three-year deal worth $3.57 million offer sheet with the Toronto Tempo in free agency and was prepared to head north to the expansion franchise. Sources in Washington claim that never was going to happen -- she was a restricted free agent, and the Mystics were ready to match any offer -- but Austin, the only player remaining from the previous regime, was considering her options.

First, though, she wanted to have a conversation with Johnson. For all of 2024, the team's record was essentially an afterthought; the new coach wanted to focus on building a cultural foundation. Johnson emphasized he wanted the team to play with "joy" more than anything else -- so often that it became a running joke, as the coach would work "joy" into nearly every conversation ad nauseum.

Austin understood the rebuild ahead, but heading into her fifth season, she wanted to play for more than just joy and felt that Johnson was being a bit "timid" in Year 1.

"Do you want to just be okay with being okay, or do you want to go out there and see what the [expletive] we can do?" Austin said. "I'm just too competitive to allow us to settle, in a sense. I really had to talk with Coach.

"If they were to bring me back, I just truly wanted to be like, okay, we have enough players that we can be better than last year and we can still strive for success."

Austin wasn't alone with those feelings. Citron and Iriafen wanted more, too.

And while Johnson and the team have embraced his good-natured "girl dad" persona, they also didn't want to compete for a participation trophy. This season, the fiery side of Johnson began to appear more often. In a 32-point loss to the Atlanta Dream in early June, he had to be escorted off the court by three police officers after being ejected. Team security, three assistant coaches and Iriafen all failed to corral Johnson as he unleashed fury.

"It was really important to go into Year 2 withholding that we're going to have our joy, but we're also going to be competitive and ruthless in competition and merge those two," Johnson said. "Positive competitiveness is how I phrase it. It doesn't have to be like s---ty, crappy behavior in the sake of winning. 'The end justifies the means?' I don't believe in that.

"When our players -- Kira and Kiki and Sonia, especially -- were like, Coach, you can push us more -- all right, now we're off and running."

With their stars on board, the front office was selective about what veterans to bring in as it looked to construct the roster this offseason. They didn't want to stunt the growth of the youngsters, but if they were going to shoot for the playoffs, some experience was necessary. Michaela Onyenwere, 27, spent 2025 in Chicago, where Johnson was an assistant, so there was already a relationship and knowledge about the type of example she would be.

The organization was wary about the same things at the trade deadline and declined to make a move. But when the New York Liberty waived Betnijah Laney-Hamilton, who never found a consistent role under new coach Chris DeMarco, the Mystics pounced. The one-time All-Star, two-time all-defense selection, 2020 Most Improved Player and 2024 champion was Onyenwere's veteran when she entered the league as a rookie in New York. Onyenwere said she would be a perfect fit.

Laney-Hamilton proved that immediately. Before even being made active, she was leaning into huddles midgame and making her voice heard. Then games and a cookout were held at her home in Vegas during a road trip to face the Aces.

"What's really unique is just the energy in the environment," Laney-Hamilton said. "The environment that's been created, just the culture of the team, has been really great.

"It's just like this newfound energy. I feel like just a weight off my shoulders to just be somewhere different, be somewhere just being embraced and all the things."

THE PRACTICE SIDE of CareFirst Arena -- the building that serves as the Mystics' and G-League Capital City Go-Go's home arena and the practice facility for both teams and the Wizards -- features two full-length courts and six baskets. Center court on one side features the Wizards logo; the Mystics crest is on the other. Championship banners for both franchises are mounted against the far wall; panels above the court mimic the red and white Washington D.C. flag.

Before every Mystics practice comes individual work for each player, who is matched up with her own specific coach. On this day, Citron dribbles a basketball with one hand while dribbling a tennis ball in the other. She and assistant coach Clinton Crouch, with his trademark hoodie pulled up over his head, go through a variety of drills. Iriafen and assistant coach Barb Turner, the leading dancer among the staff, focus on footwork in the post.

Individual work with assistant coaches isn't unique, but it is a daily part of Monumental's development program. Another cornerstone has become what they call "decimal meetings." Approximately once each quarter, every player has a group session with the head coach, performance coach and representatives from the medical staff, executive staff, research & development, analytics, mental health and physical therapy. The goal is to use data to focus on each player's individual growth. They specifically track a variety of data points in and out of games to set goals on where and how to improve, then measure how that's coming along.

Iriafen, for example, wasn't happy with her progress earlier in the season, but the meetings proved that she was ahead of 2025.

"I'm just like an analytical nerd," she explained. "So, to see the numbers, I'm like, OK, maybe the eye test [felt] like this, but the numbers show you're trending in the right directions.

"Decimals have been really helpful to just have the facts in front of you. There's so many ways you can have your emotions play into things, but the facts don't lie."

The Mystics just implemented the decimal system this season, adapted from a version that the Wizards have used in previous seasons. That ended up being an advantage for the Mystics, after the structure went through trial and error with the men. Certain things worked; others didn't. Some of the metrics were evaluated and their importance adjusted.

There's a hesitancy to say the Mystics are simply mimicking the system applied by the Wizards, but there are core philosophical beliefs and standards that Winger and his staff consider vital to building successful basketball teams, so there is some crossover. On the Mystics' side, the rebuild has been quicker and the depths of the losing nowhere near as low.

"You have two franchises in the same building and a lot of the resources are shared resources," said John Thompson III, the senior vice president of Monumental Basketball. "That relates to actual physical space as well as the mental resources and capacity of the people in the building. Without a doubt, learning, watching, growing as the Wizards have gone through their version of the decimals, it made it much easier to transfer over and know exactly what we wanted to accomplish and how we wanted to accomplish and go about our player development."

The results on the court have been impressive, with the biggest difference on the defensive end. The Mystics are currently No. 3 in the league in defensive rating and No. 2 in points allowed. Last season they were ninth in both. A healthy Austin is the anchor, currently the No. 1 player in the league defending shots in the restricted area, according to Second Spectrum. Citron has grown into one of the top perimeter defenders as she guarded more shots against 2026 All-Stars than any other perimeter player in the league, according to Second Spectrum. The front office also specifically targeted bigger, stronger, more athletic players during the offseason to help things on the defensive end of the floor.

Offensively, Washington ranks No. 13 in the league (82.8 points per game), but it has beaten every playoff team at least once this season thanks to a physical, stifling defense.

"We want to be someone known for being just a team you don't want to go up against," Citron said. "Togetherness and toughness, that's our two pillars for what we want to be known as a team."

THE DANCE PARTIES might break out at any time on this team, but only one person shuts them down. Like with many teams in the league, the Mystics social media team records everyone heading to the locker room after victories. Turner is usually first in the tunnel with a side-to-side bop. But it's Johnson that goes viral. Once it was an all-out belly flop onto the locker room floor. There was a leaping fist pump with a landing on his knees. Once he stormed in making a windmill with his arms before a shake of his rear end. There was a spin with a Michael Jackson kick. He even once sprinted in with a bag of balls for a mock game of dodgeball. A side-to-side, hands-up motion with Amoore felt like an inside joke that is difficult to describe.

"He is a dad coach," Iriafen said. "He gets, in the most respectful, loving way, cringier every time. We are his kids' age, so I think it's really cool for him to like go home and be with his kids and then come to work and have like 15 daughters."

Austin added, "He does it to be goofy with the girls, and they think it's cringe half the time, but everybody loves it."

This is the balance that Johnson works to achieve. Until Laney-Hamilton was added, the Mystics were the youngest team in the league. There's an energy that comes with a roster that is barely able to legally drink alcohol. And Johnson has adapted.

"I'm just trying to fit in with this crew," Johnson said. "Why are we doing this if we can't celebrate gains, daily gains and then big moments?

"If we can't enjoy that, then it's wasted to me. So, when I see their youthful exuberance and I see them dancing or dubs in the chat or phrasing how they call themselves -- which I'm not gonna call them -- it rubs off. It's almost like they're giving me a license to join in."

That's where this Mystics team lives -- a balance between a young silliness and a seriousness on the court. Somehow, that has turned into a playoff team that's well ahead of schedule. And the party is never far away.

stories.headline: Judging Premier League overreactions: Title race down to Arsenal and Man City?
stories.summary: Let's overreact to last weekend's Premier League action, from Arsenal and Man City separating from the pack to the VAR controversies on everyone's minds.
stories.body:
Despite seeing some breathtaking action in the Premier League over the past few days, it was another weekend dominated by talk of VAR and officiating. More on that later, but it was a round where Manchester City and Arsenal both got wins on the road, Hull City continued to impress, Tottenham Hotspur failed to score again and Coventry City were humbled at home.

There are plenty of takes around after the weekend, and ahead of the next batch of fixtures we look at some snap judgements before weighing up whether they are overreactions or legit takes.

Let's start with the two teams that have separated themselves at the top of the table.

Jump to:

Title-race contenders already decided?

Newly promoted clubs even better than last year's?

VAR in need of an overhaul?

Spurs to battle relegation ... again?

Coventry's Lampard not up to PL standard?

The title race is already down to just two teams

With two teams getting four straight wins to start the season, the top of the league has a familiar look. Defending champions Arsenal and Manchester City, who won their most recent title in 2024, have opened up a four-point lead between themselves and fourth-place Hull. The league looks certain to end up either with Gunners manager Mikel Arteta or the new coach at the Etihad Stadium, Enzo Maresca.

Verdict: NOT AN OVERREACTION

Regardless of the subplots, Arsenal and Manchester City are ahead of the rest in the Premier League. Chelsea have the attack to trouble the best teams in the league, but their defense is so vulnerable, leaving Arsenal and City out on their own. Both teams have claimed all 12 available points and are setting the standard.

Arsenal needed Bruno Guimarães' wondergoal to help them past Sunderland on Saturday evening, while the controversial Erling Haaland goal gave City their 1-0 derby win over Manchester United at Old Trafford on Sunday. City's win came after having Phil Foden sent off in the first half, but their hugely impressive game management guided them home.

Arsenal have barely missed a beat since winning the league last season, and their summer recruitment has made them even sturdier. It helps when you have the outstanding David Raya in goal (who saved Enzo Le Fée's penalty) but other players are showing some eye-catching early-season form. Midfielder Martin Ødegaard is playing brilliantly, while winger Bukayo Saka is showing signs of being back to his best.

The teams around them are showing vulnerabilities. Liverpool are lacking a clinical touch under Andoni Iraola. Manchester United have made a poor start under Carrick. All the while, Arsenal and Manchester City are ticking along nicely.

This season's promoted clubs are even better than last year's

Four matches in, Ipswich Town, Hull and Coventry are arguably surpassing the achievements of last year's promoted teams already. Hull were briefly the league leaders when they pulled ahead of Chelsea during their match on Saturday, while Ipswich are 10th in the table at this early stage.

Verdict: OVERREACTION

Hull have been outstanding. They could've quite easily come away from Stamford Bridge with three points on Saturday with Mohamed-Ali Cho having a late effort well-saved by Emiliano Martínez, but their draw meant they sit on eight points from four matches. They're undefeated, laughing in the face of those who predicted they would slip straight back down to the Championship without creating much of a ripple.

At this point last year, Sunderland had seven points, one fewer than Hull's total. Sunderland would go on to finish seventh. For Hull, their aim is still the same as it was preseason: survival. Their affable manager, Sergej Jakirović, would not be convinced to make any more ambitious goals as he talked to the media after Hull's 2-2 draw at Chelsea.

Of the other promoted teams, Ipswich won 3-2 at Crystal Palace on Saturday, thanks to new signing Zian Flemming's late goal. They sit on six points, their win at Selhurst Park coupled with their opening-round triumph over Sunderland. But then there's Coventry (more on them later), who are yet to pick up a point and fell 5-0 at home to Brighton & Hove Albion on Sunday.

Compare this with last season after four rounds: Leeds United were on four points, and Burnley three alongside Sunderland's lightning start. That means of the promoted teams, they have collectively amassed 14 points from the opening four rounds. To add further perspective, this year's batch of promoted teams have collectively spent in the region of €557 million over the summer transfer window. Last year's forked out €434 million. Per million spent, last season's are faring better.

Can we make any sweeping statements about the quality of this year's teams compared to last season? It's far too early, but two things are for certain: Hull are hugely impressive, and Ipswich have started life nicely in the top flight. As for Coventry, is it time to panic?

Arteta is right: The game is unprotected

The Arsenal manager was left fuming over a controversial penalty against his team in their trip to Sunderland, while Manchester United were angry at Erling Haaland's winner -- a goal that Pro Ref, the Premier League referees' body, later said an "error of judgement" had contributed to being awarded. It's time for VAR to be overhauled as right now, it's not fit for its purpose.

Verdict: NOT AN OVERREACTION

It feels like any and every weekend comes accompanied with moaning about a VAR error. On Saturday, Arteta's Arsenal won 2-0 at Sunderland, but he was unhappy with the decision to award a penalty against his team in the second half. You can see why. Ezri Konsa was deemed to have fouled Dan Ballard at a corner. Replays showed that it was Konsa who was being fouled, Ballard putting in a judo-roll-type maneuver on him.

Postmatch, Arteta said: "We have a lot of cameras and VAR, we have to take responsibility to protect the game. Today the game was unprotected, and it could have cost us the game and the momentum which is a really, really serious thing."

His point was underlined further the next day, when Haaland's winner was somehow given despite VAR paying close attention to the whole passage of play. The goal was originally disallowed as Haaland was deemed offside. The VAR clarified he was being played onside by Patrick Dorgu. But what the VAR bafflingly decided was that City's Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the middle of the box, despite him clearly trying to head the ball under pressure from Lisandro Martínez. Both goalkeeper Senne Lammens and Martínez were distracted by Fernández, leaving Haaland free at the far post. It was a bizarre call, and soon came the admission of fault from the body ironically called Pro Ref. "It's worrying if that's how the game is seen," Manchester United manager Michael Carrick said.

Talking on the BBC after the match, former United star Wayne Rooney called it perfectly: "I'm so sick of VAR, it's horrendous. It takes all the emotion out the game, the energy that the game is played with."

Spurs will be in the relegation battle ... again

After four matches, Spurs have two points and no goals. This past weekend, they drew with Everton in a dreary 0-0. After two successive 17th-place finishes in the league, Tottenham are in for another torrid season.

Verdict: OVERREACTION

Remember last season when Aston Villa went the first five matches of the season without a win? They ended up in the fourth. When questioning Spurs' form so far, you can bracket Villa into this question, really, given they are one point worse off than Spurs: three defeats and a loss. But Unai Emery is molding a much-changed squad, and that will take time. They'll be fine.

Spurs are in the same boat. They spent €366.5 million over the summer, and they have a new-look midfield and a tenacious manager, to boot. Yes, their early-season form has been slow, and they've shown limitations in front of goal, but it will click. Sávio and Omar Marmoush will get used to Roberto De Zerbi's way, and Mohammed Kudus will play his way back into form. Meanwhile, De Zerbi is clearly working on Mathys Tel's confidence judging by their exchange on the field after their 0-0 draw with Everton on Saturday.

Their form has been a little alarming, with defeats to Brentford and Newcastle United, and a draw at Forest alongside the Everton result, but Spurs will finish in the top half of the table.

Coventry City's Frank Lampard hit his ceiling in the Championship

This was meant to be Coventry's grand return to the Premier League, back in the top flight for the first time in 25 years. But after four matches and a collective spend of €160 million, they are already under the pump. They are still without a point and yet to score a goal. Manager Frank Lampard, who has led the club since late 2024, is now under the spotlight.

Verdict: OVERREACTION

When a manager loses the fans, that's the beginning of the end. Coventry's are still behind Lampard.

They have started life in the Premier League with a 3-0 defeat at Arsenal, a 1-0 loss at home to Hull, a 1-0 defeat at Manchester City and then the 5-0 capitulation to Brighton on Sunday. The first three are explainable, but the margin of the latest loss looks alarming.

But let's take a breath. Coventry played well in the first half against Brighton, and Taiwo Awoniyi's red card in the 53rd minute effectively ended this as a contest. At that stage, Coventry were still carving out chances but were 2-0 down, chasing the match.

Lampard's Premier League record is mixed. In his first season with Chelsea (2019-20), they finished fourth, but he was gone by January 2021. He took charge of Everton in January 2022 and kept them up on the final day of the season. He was sacked by January 2023. Then came the emotional return to Chelsea: He was caretaker from April through the end of the 2022-23 season but won just one of his 11 matches.

Talk to Coventry fans, and they're still fully behind the man who led them back to the promised land. As the team gets used to the pace and physicality of the top flight, Lampard can still get things right, and Coventry's fans still believe. Just listen to the noise that greeted full time on Sunday. Boos? Not a bit of it -- Coventry's fans stood and applauded their team. It was remarkable -- but Lampard does need to find wins.

stories.headline: No stadium, no problems as Devils look to build roster
stories.summary: The Tasmania Devils chief executive has played down concerns that a contentious stadium will impact the club's ability to attract star AFL talent.
stories.body:
The Tasmania Devils believe an unfinished stadium won't hurt their prospects of luring players to the club as they prepare to announce their first batch of signings.

Speaking at Canberra's Parliament House on Tuesday, the club's chief executive Brendon Gale played down concerns surrounding the contentious Macquarie Point Stadium in Hobart.

The $1.13 billion venue won't be ready in time when the Devils' AFL and AFLW teams enter the league in 2028, and will be primed for the 2031 season.

Tasmania plans to split its home games between Hobart's Bellerive Oval and Launceston's UTAS Stadium in the first years of its AFL campaign instead.

The stadium concerns come as the club looks to land the signatures of marquee names when they are allowed to lure 18 uncontracted players from rival clubs across 2027-28.

But in a possible precursor to the challenges that lie ahead, young gun Logan Morris re-signed with Brisbane despite the Devils taking an interest in him.

Even without a state-of-the-art stadium and no Morris, Gale remains confident in their ability to recruit players to the Apple Isle.

"We have an incredible high-performance centre which is being built, and that'll be 9,000 square metres and an elite environment to come and work and realise your potential as a male or female athlete," Gale said.

"I think those things are probably more important, and I don't expect (no stadium) to have an impact on getting players at all.

"When the stadium comes along in 2031, there'll be another big sugar hit. There'll be so much anticipation, excitement again."

In the NRL, the Perth Bears have struggled to pin down a marquee player ahead of their entrance into the competition next season, while fellow expansion club PNG Chiefs have inked deals with several star names because of lucrative tax-free contracts.

Regardless, media reports have emerged the Devils will unveil their first batch of players later this month, which will be under-17 prospects, after the league allowed the team to sign a maximum of 12 under-17 athletes across 2026 and 2027.

The club's entrance is set to create another conundrum for the AFL, as it considers whether it should shorten games, as it may need to expand the number of rounds to cater for the new team.

Jack Riewoldt, a former Richmond premiership winner and Tasmanian local, said the changes were above his pay grade.

"The game continues to evolve. The rules continue to evolve to make sure not only is it safe for the players, but user experience and viewership can be at their most prevalent," he said.

stories.headline: Max vs 100: How Verstappen's karting years made an F1 champion - and prepared him for an all-new test
stories.summary: Max Verstappen tells ESPN's Laurence Edmondson how his karting roots shaped his F1 career and prepared him for the Max vs 100 challenge.
stories.body:
On Sept. 16, Max Verstappen will attempt to overtake 100 other drivers in a unique go-karting challenge at Silverstone, live on Disney+. Ahead of the event, ESPN caught up with the four-time world champion to discuss his long history of go-karting and the years he spent honing his skills at tracks across Europe.

Between the ages of four and 15, Max Verstappen's life revolved around go-kart tracks.

Weekends would be spent racing all around Europe, initially close to home in Belgium and the Netherlands and then further afield in Italy, Spain and the U.K. in his early teens.

His father, Jos, a former Formula 1 driver, would load Max's kart into the back of their van ahead of every race weekend and drive his son across the length and breadth of Europe to the next event. During the height of Max's karting career, Jos calculated they were clocking up more than 60,000 motorway miles per year as the father-and-son team hoovered up trophies on a path destined for F1.

"It was a really nice period in my life," Max recalls. "All different kinds of conditions, tracks, travels.

- Max vs 100: Meet the drivers racing against Red Bull's Verstappen

- Max vs 100: F1 drivers predict how Verstappen will fare racing 100 drivers

- What makes Max Verstappen so good? Career, background and F1 records

"Sometimes it wasn't even the race weekend I loved the most, but just the travel experience together with my dad; in the van, talking a lot about life, talking a lot about the current, but also, of course, where we were trying to head to.

"For sure, go-karting has been a massive part of my life."

On weekdays, Jos would pick Max up after school and take him directly to his workshop to work on his kart engines. Max was encouraged to get his hands dirty from an early age, and the hours of tinkering after school would only come to an end when it was time to head home for dinner. Once they'd eaten, Max would go up to bed and Jos would return to the workshop, sometimes until midnight, until every last performance advantage had been found.

"My dad was my mechanic and my engine tuner as well," Max recalls. "We had our own dyno also in the workshop, so we did a lot in-house.

"I know a lot of dads are mechanics or they work with their son, but I don't know anyone that has done it so intensively.

"My dad really understood what was needed from the go-kart, but also from the engine."

The local kart circuit in Genk, Belgium became the Verstappens' second home. All through the year Max would take to the track multiple times a week to test new parts while learning to brake later, rotate the kart more precisely, and get on the throttle earlier.

Even in the wet winter months when other karters would pack up early and go home, the Verstappens would continue to clock up the mileage. Max would stay out on track until his hands felt frozen to the bone and he could barely feel his fingertips.

"I would warm my gloves on the exhaust because it's quite hot," he says with a smile. "You could put your gloves on it for a little bit and then take them off and they would be warm.

"It works really well, but the problem is when you're really cold and you heat them up your fingers swell up because of the increase of blood flow. Sometimes you were driving a bit with thick hands. But it all makes you tougher as a driver and as a kid at the time."

'You only get one shot at this'

The school Max was attending in Belgium didn't recognise go-karting as a sport, which made it difficult to get exemptions from class for races on the other side of Europe. When he did, the young Verstappen tried to focus on his homework during those 10- or 12-hour road trips in the van, but ultimately his schoolwork never came as easily as the karting trophies.

"It was tough. Sometimes I would come back home and you arrive on a Monday back, and you've kind of missed a week of lecturing and you try to catch up within two or three days of what was missed.

"With that already I didn't like school, so it was a bit tough.

"I always targeted to do something in life where school was not necessary. Plus, at the same time, I always said to myself, even if it doesn't work out in racing I can always go back to school.

"You only get one shot at this. If you fail because you try to catch up on school, I think I would always kick myself. School you can always catch up on."

It's hard to believe now, but early in Max's karting journey there was a moment when Jos wasn't sure if his son had the talent to make it all the way to F1. He had been karting for over a year and making steady progress, but then, ahead of his sixth birthday, the lap times stopped improving.

"I think there was a time when my dad was questioning it a little bit," Max says. "We always went to that same track in Genk, and at one point I stalled a little bit -- when you are four years old naturally there is a progression, but I think around five-and-a-half or six years old it was like I plateaued. We went again and again and again and I didn't really get faster.

"I just kept being a couple of tenths off what I needed to be, of the older guys because that is what you compare yourself to. Then my dad had a good idea. We went to a different track for the first time, so I drove somewhere new for the first time.

"It actually went really well on that particular track, so when I went back to Genk it also clicked and I suddenly just picked up pace.

"Maybe my mind needed a little reset of just seeing different corners and a different combination of corners.

"I spoke about it with my dad years later, but I remember the scene of going to Genk over and over again and going to that other track for the first time, I do remember that.

"At the time I didn't know that my dad was so worried about my pace, but I do remember the sequence because it went really well on that particular track. My dad was like, 'tomorrow we go again but to Genk.' I was like 'alright, sure. I drive wherever.'"

- Max vs 100 explained: Rules, drivers, shortcuts and how Verstappen can win

Was there ever a time when Max didn't enjoy the endless pursuit of lap time?

"I always loved it and I think you always want to go out and go fast," he says.

"But of course there are also moments where maybe it's not going so well. You don't love it to 100%. But at the end of the day I would always wake up the next day wanting to go.

"It's like in life. There are better days and there are worse days."

How Jos Verstappen prepared Max for F1

In Jos, Max had a mechanic, an engineer and a driver coach. Every time they arrived for a test session, there would be a plan to ensure every lap resulted in progress towards the end goal of winning the next race, fighting for the next championship, and inching closer to the dream of F1.

"When we went karting there was always a clear strategy behind it with my dad, in terms of what we were practicing," Max says.

"My dad never said to me 'just go out and have fun.' No, we go out because we're testing or preparing. There was always a very strict strategy behind it.

"Even when we would go on summer holidays, of course we would also spend time on the beach, but we had go-karting days where we would create mini races.

"So one time I would start first, then second, third, last. With however many people we were with, which was mainly 7-8 people maximum. So one time you start first, then last, or you're in the middle.

"We would create these little start scenarios and overtaking scenarios. It was really fun."

The nostalgia Max feels for those endless days of karting is almost tangible as he sits in Red Bull's F1 paddock hospitality. The dream he had as a kid was ultimately fulfilled in 2021 when he won his first Formula 1 title before going on to take three more over the following three years.

Now a father himself, it begs the question of whether he can see himself becoming a karting dad?

"You don't know," he says. "I think what is always very important as a parent is that you support them in whatever they want to do.

"It doesn't matter if you're a boy or a girl, but for me, I'm not going to be the parent that is going to push them into a racing scenario. If they want to do it, sure. I will make sure that she or he will have the best possibilities.

"But I'm not going to actively push it. They need to want it.

"I hope they do something else -- I hope they play tennis or play football!"

Max vs 100: Can Verstappen pass them all?

The freezing cold test days and overtaking drills during his summer holidays will likely come in useful next week as Max attempts to pass 100 karts on a specially designed kart track at Silverstone. The furthest back he can remember starting on a grid during his karting career was 10th or 11th and he hasn't driven a competitive go-kart since 2016 (his track days away from F1 are now firmly focused on GT racing).

"A hundred is a lot, you know, but I think how they've set up the track from what they've shown me, I think it will be good," Max says of the challenge. "But it's still going to be hectic, for sure."

And in terms of a strategy, will Max, to borrow one of his own phrases, go "full send"?

"I think I first need to understand and see the level between drivers.

"I also don't like to overthink the situation. I just need to go with the flow and try to make the best of it.

"I'm hoping that with my background, I should be faster than most. I hope! I mean, it would be quite embarrassing if they're faster than me!"

Max vs 100: When and how do I watch it?
Max vs 100 is taking place on Sept. 16, and will be shown live in the UK on Disney+.

In the U.S., Max vs 100 will also air on the ESPN App for Unlimited subscribers before a delayed ESPN2 broadcast later that day.

The race itself will start at 6 p.m., with the live stream beginning one hour before.

Comedian Mo Gilligan will front the coverage, which is set to include drone footage and live race data.

stories.headline: Source: Colombia, U.S. battling for Inter Miami U20 dual national Alexander Shaw
stories.summary: Inter Miami midfielder Alexander Shaw has been contacted by Colombia after playing for the United States U-20 team in the 2026 Concacaf tournament, a source confirmed to ESPN.
stories.body:
Inter Miami midfielder Alexander Shaw is currently being pursued by both Colombia and the United States on a youth Under 20 level, a source confirmed to ESPN.

He previously featured for the United States youth national team in the 2026 Concacaf U20 champion, reaching the final after a perfect group stage. Shaw helped the USYNT to victories against Haiti, El Salvador and Cuba without conceding a goal.

Shaw scored in the 5-0 victory over Cuba.

The USYNT concluded the tournament as runners-up after falling 2-0 to Mexico.

Shaw has previously received call ups from the Colombia U20, but a source confirms that all requests have been declined by Inter Miami for occurring during Major League Soccer regular season action.

Shaw, however, joined the Colombian national team during the World Cup as a sparring under manager Nestor Lorenzo while the squad trained in Miami.

A source confirmed to ESPN that both Colombia and the United States are looking for Shaw to join the team for the upcoming U-20 World Cup in 2027.

Inter Miami recently signed Shaw to a contract through the end of the 2026 MLS season, with options to extend through June 2027, the 2027-28 and 2028-29 seasons.

He's made five appearances this season and recorded a goal in the 7-1 victory over CF Montreal.

stories.headline: Roosters make Walker call as half's absence laid bare
stories.summary: James Tedesco says Daly Cherry-Evans took ownership of his off night against Penrith, as the Sydney Roosters aim to knock Cronulla out of the finals.
stories.body:
James Tedesco claims it would be unfair to lay the blame for the Sydney Roosters' last-gasp finals loss to Penrith at the feet of veteran halfback Daly Cherry-Evans.

As the Roosters resisted the urge to rush Sam Walker back for Saturday's sudden-death semi-final with Cronulla, Tedesco revealed how Cherry-Evans had shouldered the blame for last Sunday's 19-12 defeat to the Panthers.

Cherry-Evans gave away a seven-tackle set in the final 10 minutes with Penrith halfback Nathan Cleary converting a field goal soon afterwards.

The 37-year-old Cherry-Evans then sprayed his own attempt wide when his side needed him to stay calm under pressure, which sent the Roosters into a sudden-death final against the Sharks.

"Straight away he accepted it, and as a team, you don't dump that all on him," Tedesco said.

"He's done that numerous times earlier in the year and nailed it in getting us where we needed to.

"But with Chez, with his experience and how comfortable he is in those situations, we have full confidence in whatever he decides to do.

"We know he's kicked a lot, but he's missed a few as well.

"I think with Chez's experience and his age, you can't hold on to those things. I think that's important for all of us."

Walker, meanwhile, has been left on ice for a further week after coach Trent Robinson had hinted the Queensland No. 7 was an outside chance of returning against Cronulla.

The 24-year-old Walker underwent ankle surgery after suffering a syndesmosis in a loss to the Dolphins last month.

"It's only been a couple of weeks, so he's probably got another week or so I'm guessing," Tedesco said.

"But he started to do some running, which is really quick after surgery, so we'll just see how he goes in progressing to give himself a chance."

Walker's absence means the Roosters will again be without one of their most dynamic threats when they face the Sharks with Robinson forced to rely on the relatively untested partnership of Cherry-Evans and Hugo Savala.

With the first-choice halves pairing of Walker and Cherry-Evans, the Roosters have scored at a tick over 26 points per game this season.

But with Savala and Cherry-Evans as a playmaking duo, Robinson's sides are scoring an average of just 16 points per game across three fixtures.

"He (Savala) has done his job and that's all we can ask, and that's why we love playing with him," Tedesco said.

"He'll do whatever it takes for the team, we love him as a person, as a player, and he's only going to keep getting better.

Sept. 15: Tuesday's news to know
By Todd Zola

All 15 of today's games will be under the lights. Action gets underway with a quartet of 6:40 p.m. ET starts.

Miami Marlins closer Pete Fairbanks left last night's game after throwing just six pitches. The reason isn't official, but Marlins manager Clayton McCullough indicated that Fairbanks experienced a similar feeling to when he was diagnosed with medial nerve irritation -- a lingering condition that he's already suffered twice this season and requires an IL stint. If that is indeed the case, he'd be done for the season.
Spencer Miles is slated to be the bulk reliever for the Toronto Blue Jays tonight when they host the Detroit Tigers. He has served in many roles this season, including as an opener and a traditional starter, but he hasn't tossed more than 50 pitches in any single outing since late July. Miles' last appearance was on Saturday, when he opened the game, logging 44 pitches over two innings.
The Tigers could be without Colt Keith for tonight's tilt at the Rogers Centre. The infielder was scratched from the series opener last night due to a sore left thumb. He's scheduled for further evaluation today, after which his status for tonight and beyond should be clarified.
Michael Soroka and Zac Gallen will tag-team tonight's mound duties for the Arizona Diamondbacks when they face the Marlins in the desert. It doesn't appear to be a traditional opener/primary pitcher scenario, nor is it piggybacking, as Soroka is expected to handle a normal starter's workload, then have Gallen come in from the bullpen. Both veterans recently returned from the 15-day IL, but manager Torey Lovullo feels that Soroka has more swing-and-miss potential.
Kyle Freeland is set to come off the 15-day IL and start tonight's NL West tilt between the Colorado Rockies and the San Diego Padres at Coors Field. He's been out just over three weeks because of a finger issue. The lefty made one rehab start, compiling just 47 pitches for Double-A Hartford, so he'll likely be on a pitch count this evening.

Be sure to check out the latest fantasy lineup advice as well as the MLB betting tips for Tuesday.

Sept. 14: Monday's news to know

By Todd Zola

There are 10 evening games on today's abbreviated slate. Action gets underway at 6:40 p.m. ET with a pair of contests.

One of the early games features the Chicago White Sox visiting the Cleveland Guardians. The White Sox will open the divisional matchup with lefty Sean Newcomb before tagging in righty Sean Burke. Lefty-swinging Steven Kwan and Chase DeLauter are generally in the upper third of the Guardians order. Newcomb is significantly more effective when facing left-handers, while Burke's OPS versus lefties is almost 100 points higher than it is facing righties. The White Sox enter the three-game series with a one-game lead over the Guardians in the AL Central.
The Guardians will counter with Gavin Williams, who will be taking the hill after seven days of rest. He's not hurt -- the club simply opted to give him extra time between starts. His pitch counts have been running high, in part due to 11 double-digit strikeout games this season, including his last two and three of his previous four.
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts indicated that Freddie Freeman would miss tonight's series opener with the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park. The veteran first baseman has been nursing a lingering knee injury. He will likely receive multiple maintenance days over the final two weeks of the regular season. Enrique Hernandez is the primary candidate to handle first base when Freeman is on the bench.
Royce Lewis left yesterday's contest in the top of the sixth inning due to a sore left shoulder. Playing first base has kept the oft-injured infielder relatively healthy and productive. He's considered to be day-to-day heading into tonight's action as the Minnesota Twins host the New York Yankees.
Somewhat abruptly, the San Francisco Giants announced that Rafael Devers has been placed on the 60-day IL and is slated for season-ending surgery to address a core muscle injury. He'll end the year batting .258/.340/.525 with 37 home runs, one shy of his career-high.
The Colorado Rockies open a 10-game homestand tonight against the San Diego Padres. It's their longest stretch at Coors Field for the season and marks one of the few weeks where they play seven home games during a single fantasy scoring period.
The Miami Marlins will be without Owen Caissie for at least 10 days -- and possibly the season -- after placing him on the 10-day IL as a result of a lumbar stress reaction. Contact remains troubling for the outfielder as his 37.3% strikeout rate fueled a .220/.288/.412 line. Esteury Ruiz will likely see additional playing time. Caissie's roster spot was filled by Xavier Edwards, who returned from the IL and will be reinserted as the team's regular second baseman.

Be sure to check out the latest fantasy lineup advice as well as the MLB betting tips for Monday.

Sept. 13: Sunday's news to know

By Todd Zola

It's another early Sunday start with the Detroit Tigers entertaining the Colorado Rockies at 12:10 p.m. ET. The usual 13 matinees follow, with the San Francisco Giants hosting the San Diego Padres in the evening game.

The rubber game between the Boston Red Sox and Kansas City Royals at Fenway Park has been moved from 1:35 p.m. ET to 3:05 p.m. ET to avoid early afternoon storms in the area. The Royals could have Jac Caglianone returning to the starting lineup after he was able to pinch-hit in yesterday's contest. The slugger had missed the previous five games due to a left flexor strain.
The Minnesota Twins promoted top prospect Emmanuel Rodriguez in advance of yesterday's home date with the Cleveland Guardians. He responded by delivering a homer in his first career plate appearance. The 23-year-old outfielder generated a .262/.414/.500 line in his 49 games with Triple-A St. Paul. Rodriguez will likely play regularly down the stretch, but will also maintain 2027 rookie status.
The Texas Rangers lineup received a boost after the team activated Josh Jung from the IL. He's been out since just after the All-Star break thanks to a strained calf. Jung's return is timely as the Rangers sit just two games behind the Houston Astros for the AL West lead. They're also in play for the third AL wild card. Jung is batting .295/.362/.440, albeit in just 93 games.
The Athletics are playing out the string, but they'll be doing it with catcher Shea Langeliers serving as the team's DH. He underwent meniscus surgery in July, but the recovery went well. Even so, Langeliers isn't expected to play behind the plate again this season.
The Pittsburgh Pirates will be without Esmerlyn Valdez for at least 10 days and possibly the rest of the season, after placing him on the IL due to a left hamstring strain. The outfielder has emerged as one of the club's top run producers over the second half, though he'd been struggling lately. Even so, Valdez clubbed three homers and a double over his last 11 games, helping soften a 39% strikeout rate and a .154 average over that span.

stories.headline: Boston Celtics offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: It was an offseason of change for the Celtics. Can they still compete in the upgraded Eastern Conference?
stories.body:
It didn't take long for the Boston Celtics to make noise this offseason, as the historic franchise decided to trade 2024 Finals MVP Jaylen Brown to the rival Philadelphia 76ers on July 6 for Paul George and a collection of future picks.

The trade came on the heels of the Celtics missing out on two-time All-Star Giannis Antetokounmpo, who was moved to the Miami Heat after a heavy pursuit from Boston at the start of the summer.

The Celtics will now be fully in the hands of Jayson Tatum, who returned late last season from a torn Achilles in the 2025 playoffs. Tatum will be joined by George and fresh signings Mitchell Robinson and Mike Conley.

Will the moves be enough for the Celtics to compete in the East? Or will moving on from Jaylen Brown prove too costly in a strengthened Eastern Conference?

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Friday. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for all 30 teams.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Celtics coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: Paul George, Mitchell Robinson, Mike Conley

Key subtractions: Jaylen Brown, Nikola Vucevic

Key retentions: Neemias Queta, Jordan Walsh, Ron Harper Jr.

Boston responded to its first early playoff exit since 2021 by boldly trading Brown to the 76ers, ending his fruitful partnership with Jayson Tatum. The move should improve the Celtics' long-term flexibility to build around Tatum, but next year's iteration will require the aging George to discover the fountain of youth. The 36-year-old forward has played in 60 games just once in the past seven seasons.

Even so, this shouldn't be viewed as a gap year. The Celtics return a cohesive nucleus, and they added Robinson's defense and rebounding to shore up a frontcourt rotation that was overwhelmed in the postseason.

If Tatum returns to superstar form in his first fully healthy season since a May 2025 Achilles injury, the Celtics will have a chance to win at least 50 games for the sixth straight year. Securing Banner 19, however, will likely require finding a superstar replacement for Brown sometime down the road. -- Ben Golliver

Zach Kram's offseason grade: C-

The Celtics undercut the Knicks with their addition of Mitchell Robinson and signed Neemias Queta to a great extension. But their offseason will be defined by the stunning Jaylen Brown trade, which shocked the basketball world not because it happened but because it brought back such a light return from the 76ers (Paul George, two first-round picks and two second-round picks) for the player who finished sixth in MVP voting last season.

So many aspects of the Brown trade -- from his fit in Philadelphia to the value of George's contract to what the trade says about analytics and the NBA's financial landscape -- will continue to be debated for months, if not years.

President of basketball operations Brad Stevens might prove correct in the long run. But right now, it seems like the Celtics reduced their 2026-27 championship equity without saving all that much money, so they receive one of my worst offseason grades. -- Kram

What we learned over the past few months
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: The second apron can break hearts.

The NBA's harsh second apron penalties and restrictions have caused multiple contenders to shed salary and lose talent. This summer, the 2025 champion Oklahoma City Thunder traded away Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe, and the reigning champion New York Knicks watched Mitchell Robinson leave in free agency.

But no apron-related move sparked an outcry like the Celtics' decision to trade Jaylen Brown to the 76ers for Paul George, two first-round picks and two second-round picks. The 2024 Finals MVP had spent 10 seasons in Boston, reached six Eastern Conference finals, earned five All-Star selections and fostered deep connections with the local community. With that track record, it was hard for fans to view Brown as just another line in the spreadsheet.

But NBA commissioner Adam Silver was unsentimental when asked about the second apron's impacts in Las Vegas last week. Silver said that moves like the Brown trade were "certainly not an unintended consequence" of the apron rules, adding that "people need to manage budgets" and teams "can't have unlimited resources." In other words, any upset Celtics fans should wipe their tears and deal with the league's new economic reality. -- Golliver

The big question: How will the Celtics' offense function without Brown?
Brown peaked as an offensive force while carrying the Celtics through Tatum's absence for much of last season: He averaged career highs in points, shot attempts, and assists, and his 36.2 usage rate ranked second in the NBA. Even though Tatum played only 16 games, Boston finished with the league's second-best offensive rating.

A healthy Tatum will help fill some of the void created by Brown's departure, but Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla will also seek to craft the right roles for George and Payton Pritchard within an offensive system that generates lots of 3-point attempts and limits turnovers.

George's reliable outside shooting should ease his transition to Boston, which ranked fourth in 3-point attempts last season and is sure to give him the green light. Expect Pritchard, a nifty scorer who shifted between starting and bench roles last season, to build on his career year in 2025-26 with expanded opportunities. -- Golliver

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 4
Here are the predicted Net Points per 100 possessions for the Celtics' top seven players for the 2026-27 season:

If you never lose more than three games in a row, players are going to listen to you. That's what Joe Mazzulla has accomplished as coach of the Celtics for three years now, despite so much turnover in their rotation. Losing streaks eat at players and coaches, allowing some nasty inner voices to surface. But three games? That's a blip that they can all move past really quickly and keep focusing on the process. -- Dean Oliver

Read about how Net Points works here.

Biggest X factor
Mitchell Robinson

Due to a focus on winning the possession battle, by avoiding turnovers and crashing the offensive glass, the Celtics led the league in shot attempts per 100 possessions last season. And now they've added the best offensive rebounder in the NBA, with Robinson crossing sides in the Knicks-Celtics rivalry in free agency.

Robinson's health will always be a concern, but when he's on the court in Boston, he should help Joe Mazzulla's team strengthen its possession focus and generate plenty of open 3-pointers when he kicks out to the perimeter after grabbing offensive boards. -- Kram

Fantasy insight from our expert
Fantasy insight ahead of the season: The Celtics had led the NBA in 3-point attempts and 3-pointers made for two straight seasons before last season, when they finished fourth in attempts and third in makes. Their drop from 48.2 3-point attempts per game in 2024-25 to 42.1 3PA/G last season was likely influenced by the injury absence of Jayson Tatum (9.1 3PA/G for last three seasons) for most of the season with the offense built more around Jaylen Brown's mid-range game (5.7 3PA/G for last three seasons). But Tatum is back full time, and Brown was traded this offseason for Paul George (8.0 3PA/G over the past eight seasons). Expect the Celtics as a team to bounce back to the league lead in 3-pointers, with all of their fantasy contributing shooters maximizing their 3-pointers made. -- Andre Snellings

stories.headline: Blackhawks name Bedard, 21, franchise's 2nd-youngest captain
stories.summary: The Blackhawks named Connor Bedard, 21, as captain, the second-youngest captain in franchise history. Jonathan Toews was 20 when he received the honor.
stories.body:
The Chicago Blackhawks named Connor Bedard captain on Tuesday.

Bedard, 21, is the second-youngest captain in franchise history. Jonathan Toews was 20 when he received the honor.

"Connor perfectly embodies what it means to be a Blackhawk," Blackhawks general manager Kyle Davidson said in a statement. "From the moment he entered the League, Connor has led by example and has set a remarkable standard for himself while demonstrating his ability to make the players around him better."

Chicago won the NHL draft lottery and selected Bedard No. 1 in 2023, its first No. 1 pick since Patrick Kane in 2007. The Canadian-born center immediately became the centerpiece of the team's rebuild -- which is expected to accelerate this season, especially after re-signing Kane this summer. The Blackhawks have made the playoffs just once since 2017, and that was a first-round exit during the COVID bubble after making it through the qualifying round.

Bedard is expected to miss the beginning of this season after sustaining a shoulder injury during offseason workouts in Vancouver. After undergoing surgery, Bedard is expected to return around November.

"The captains who have come before me have left an incredible legacy. To now have the opportunity to carry that tradition forward is something I don't take lightly," Bedard said in a statement. "We're building something really special here, and I'm committed to making the entire Blackhawks organization and our fans proud."

The Blackhawks made a major commitment to Bedard this summer, inking him to a massive second contract: five years, $75 million ($15M AAV).

Bedard has led Chicago in points in each of his three seasons so far, despite adversity such as a broken jaw as a rookie. Bedard still won the Calder Trophy that season.

He reached 200 career points on April 6, becoming the first Blackhawk ever to reach 200 at age 20 or younger and only the 13th NHL player to accomplish the feat.

stories.headline: Allianz Arena to host 2028 Champions League final, Camp Nou to host in 2029
stories.summary: The Munich Football Arena and Barcelona's Spotify Camp Nou will host the 2028 and 2029 UEFA Champions League finals, European football's governing body confirmed Tuesday.
stories.body:
The Munich Football Arena and Barcelona's Spotify Camp Nou will host the 2028 and 2029 UEFA Champions League finals, European football's governing body confirmed Tuesday.

Bayern Munich's stadium -- also known as the Allianz Arena for sponsorship reasons -- held the 2025 and 2012 finals, but it will be the first time in exactly 30 years that Camp Nou has been the venue for the biggest game in European club football.

Camp Nou last hosted the final in 1999, when Manchester United famously scored two late goals to beat Bayern 2-1 to claim the second of their three European Cups.

While the 70,000-capacity Allianz Arena is ready to go, Camp Nou is still being redeveloped as part of a revamp which began in 2023.

After over two years playing away from their home stadium, Barça returned to Camp Nou last November, but work is still ongoing.

The capacity is currently capped at 62,000, with the third tier yet to be completed and the roof still to be put on.

Barça estimate that the stadium, which will eventually hold 105,000 fans, will be finished towards the end of 2027 -- or at the latest by 2028.
